title: Huma Qureshi Picks Up a Red Umbrella and a Body Count. The Baby Do Die Do Trailer Just Made the Year's Most Dangerous Woman Deaf, Mute and Unstoppable.
excerpt: India's first desi hitwoman can only hear her dead sister's voice — and she's coming to a screen near you on July 3. Her brother produced it. The trailer dropped this morning and the internet is already obsessed with the red umbrella.
body:
She doesn't say a word. That's the first thing you notice. The **Baby Do Die Do** trailer, which landed this morning, opens on a woman threading through a rain-soaked Mumbai with a blood-red umbrella, utterly unbothered by the chaos she leaves behind. By the time you realize she's the killer the whole city is hunting, **Huma Qureshi** has already owned every frame without uttering a syllable. It's a flex. A deaf-and-mute contract killer who hears only her dead sister's voice — and Qureshi plays her not as a victim of silence but as someone who weaponized it.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=2rQCZKoaEhc</youtube>

This is the kind of role actors wait a career for, and Qureshi clearly knows it. As Baby KarMarKar, she is by turns feral, funny, and genuinely frightening, swinging from slapstick to slaughter in the same breath. The trailer leans into a neo-noir palette — neon wet streets, smeared lipstick reds, the grimy gold of a Mumbai that never sleeps — shot by cinematographer **Tojo Xavier** like a fever dream that occasionally remembers it's a comedy. Because that's the gamble here: this is a crime *comedy*, a tonal high-wire act that India rarely attempts and even more rarely lands.

> "I've seen you live this role. Through the madness, the silence, the chaos — you didn't just act in this film… you became it." — Saqib Saleem, on his sister Huma

The story behind the camera is almost as juicy as the one on screen. **Baby Do Die Do** is the debut production of **Saleem Siblings**, the banner founded by Qureshi and her brother, actor-producer **Saqib Saleem**. He's been carrying this one like a torch — when the teaser first surfaced, dropped quietly as what he cheekily called a "sneaky link," he wrote his sister a love letter of a caption: "Big screen. Big scale. Big risk. And you're right at the center of it owning every frame." There's something irresistible about a brother betting his first production on his sister being the most magnetic thing in the room. Spoiler: she is.


Director **Nachiket Samant** has surrounded Qureshi with a deliciously offbeat ensemble. **Sikandar Kher** brings his particular brand of menace as Zafar, **Chunky Pandey** turns up doing what Chunky Pandey does best, and the reliably brilliant **Seema Pahwa** anchors the madness. Even the PM of India gets a cameo in this universe. The whole thing crackles with the energy of a film that knows it's strange and refuses to apologize for it.

Then there's the music. The trailer's signature track, *Gardi*, composed by **Arjun Iyer**, is the kind of unhinged, syllable-tumbling earworm that's going to live rent-free in everyone's head — "Kitni gardi hai!" half-sung, half-snarled over the carnage. It's the sonic equivalent of Baby herself: chaotic, claustrophobic, and weirdly seductive. You won't be able to unhear it, which is exactly the point.

What makes this one worth circling on the calendar is how rare its protagonist is. Bollywood's leading women have fought, flown, and led spy franchises — Alia Bhatt's **Alpha** is proof the female action lead has finally arrived. But a disabled woman as the gleeful engine of a stylized killing spree, neither pitied nor sanitized? That's new. Qureshi, who has spent years being one of Hindi cinema's most underrated talents, looks like she's finally been handed a part big enough to match her.

For the diaspora, the where-to-watch is straightforward, at least to start: **Baby Do Die Do** hits cinemas worldwide on **July 3, 2026**, a Cinépolis release, which means the usual overseas theatrical chains across the US, UK, and Canada should carry it on opening weekend — expect screenings in the NRI strongholds of New Jersey, the Bay Area, Toronto, and London. An OTT home will almost certainly follow within the customary four-to-eight-week window, though the makers haven't named a streamer yet. Given the Saleem Siblings' indie scrappiness, a digital deal announcement closer to release wouldn't surprise anyone.

The red umbrella, the silence, the body count — it's a bold, peculiar, gorgeously mounted swing at something Bollywood doesn't usually risk. Whether audiences embrace a heroine who murders in mime is the open question. But if the trailer is any guide, Huma Qureshi just delivered the performance no one will be able to look away from this summer. Don't tell her sister told you.
